name: Dana Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, technology firms, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Dana Bauer, 58, and I’m still one of the junior hands on the line crew. I came into it late with a vocational certificate, so I’m usually carrying gear, checking the ground crew’s setup, and doing repairs under a more experienced worker’s eye. I like seeing the lamps come back on along Orchard Road. The hard part is being slow at the newer equipment when everybody is already tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I’d say the computer can tidy forms, but it cannot hold a ladder steady in rain. I would still ask the company to keep a person checking every repair ticket. Our crew has enough real faults without chasing a bad entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I’m already watching every grocery receipt. My partner works at the hardware shop, and those wages won’t cover our rent and heating if my hours slip. We’ve got less than a month put aside, even if AI stays small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d turn up for my scheduled shifts and keep learning the new insulated clamps from Jo, our senior hand. Starting now, I’d stop buying lunch at the depot and take sandwiches; in the first year of a plateau I’d keep that routine and put any spare notes against our heating bill. I’m not opening a new account or claiming I can save much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is some relief because nobody is talking about replacing the crew. Still, the rent comes every month whether a machine is clever or not. I’d call it uneasy rather than comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention the heating bill. What happened last winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We paid it late twice after my hours dropped during a quiet spell. I borrowed a little from our grown son once, and I hated asking him. He has his own household now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your public line leave anything out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the part about being frightened of ordinary lost hours. At work I sound firm because the younger crew need me steady. At home I count the shifts on the calendar.

say: I’d say **human checking** still belongs on every repair ticket.
I’d tell the crew that **line faults** still need hands on site.
think: I worry about **lost hours** even if the software barely changes.
My partner’s **shop pay** cannot cover the whole household.
do: Keep taking **scheduled line shifts** and practise the insulated clamps with Jo.
Pack **depot lunches** and use the money against the heating bill.
feel: Relieved about the **crew**, yet uneasy about monthly bills.
S0.quote: My partner works at the hardware shop, and those wages won’t cover our rent and heating if my hours slip.
fieldNote: Dana contrasts her confident **depot voice** with private counting of shifts on the calendar.
A late **heating payment** and borrowing from her grown son explain her worry before any major AI change.

steps.text: Keep scheduled line shifts and practise insulated clamps with Jo
Pack depot lunches and apply the difference to heating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the planners can use software, but somebody must still see the pole and the traffic before we climb. I’d ask them to show us the new job sheets instead of dropping them on us at dawn. I’m not going to cheer for losing dispatchers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this might start with fewer office people and then fewer crews sent out. If the company can schedule tighter and leave vacancies empty, a junior worker like me loses the extra shifts first. The hands-on repair stays, but my pay could shrink long before a robot touches a wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d ask the crew lead which jobs are forecast to disappear and request to shadow Jo on fault finding. I’d keep my line shifts; in the first year after the planning system spreads, I’d apply for any local ground-crew opening if my overtime falls. I’d also drop our paid television service before touching the rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cross for the dispatchers and worried for our own kitchen table. We can adjust a little, but less overtime means an unpaid bill very quickly. I would be anxious even if the company calls it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which pay would you miss first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend callouts. I used two of those last month to clear an old fuel bill. Without them I’m back to choosing which notice to open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new planning screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they require it, I’ll learn the buttons someone shows me. I have never used an AI tool on my own and I’m slow with unfamiliar screens. I would rather learn the fault itself from Jo.

say: I’d insist **site checks** remain part of line jobs.
I’d ask for **clear job sheets** before crews leave the depot.
think: Tighter scheduling could remove my **weekend callouts** first.
I could lose **pay** without a robot doing the repair.
do: Ask the lead about **lost work** and shadow Jo on fault finding.
Apply for a **local ground-crew opening** if overtime falls.
Cancel **paid television** before rent falls behind.
feel: Cross for dispatchers and **anxious** about bills.
S1.quote: The hands-on repair stays, but my pay could shrink long before a robot touches a wire.
fieldNote: Dana sees the **office changes** reaching her through scheduling and overtime, despite low direct thinking-AI exposure.
She accepts required screens reluctantly, while **fault-finding practice** feels more useful to her than AI lessons.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and shadow Jo on fault finding
Apply for local ground-crew openings if overtime falls
Cancel the household paid television service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we need the dates on paper: thinking work by 2028 and capable line robots around 2031. I would ask the company whether it intends to keep crews between those dates. A slogan about opportunity will not pay a rent bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office jobs could vanish first and the field jobs follow three years later. I’ll be 60 when the thinking system arrives and 63 when the robots do line repairs. With less than a month saved, I cannot assume retirement will carry me across a lost wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask my supervisor for a written account of how long our line crew is budgeted, and I’d put in for paid safety-inspection training only if it leads to a local job. I’d keep working every assigned shift. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for the company’s inspection openings and ask our grown son whether he could help with rent if my hours collapse; by 2031 I’d look for any paid local maintenance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one wakes me at night. I can picture the van still pulling out while I’m left at home with a rent notice. I’m alarmed because I expect a big wage loss before I’m ready to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner after a meeting with management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner exactly what they wrote, or admit if they wrote nothing. We’d put the rent, heating and food on one page. My partner’s shop shift cannot replace my line wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enrol. We cannot pay for a course while my wage is uncertain, and I won’t pretend a certificate creates a vacancy. I’d still apply for real openings.

say: I’d ask for **written dates** for crews and robot plans.
I’d say **rent** requires a real answer, not opportunity talk.
think: At 63, I expect **line robots** to threaten my main wage.
Our **thin savings** cannot bridge lost pay to retirement.
do: Request a **written crew budget** and keep assigned shifts.
Enrol in **paid inspection training** only if it leads to local work.
Apply for **inspection or maintenance openings** and ask our son about emergency rent help.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely wage loss and sleepless nights.
S2.quote: A slogan about opportunity will not pay a rent bill.
fieldNote: Dana separates **2028 desk losses** from the later 2031 threat to physical line repair.
Her **training condition** is specific: it must be paid and connected to a real local vacancy.
She considers asking her grown son for **rent help**, although she disliked needing him before.

steps.text: Keep assigned line shifts while requesting the written crew budget
Enrol in paid safety-inspection training only with a local job path
Apply for company inspection and local maintenance openings
Ask grown son for emergency rent help if hours collapse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people five years is enough time for an honest crew-by-crew plan. The company should say what work the machines will actually do and who will be taught another job. I would not promise that every worker can simply become a supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 63 at the thinking change and 66 when line robots arrive in 2034. That is closer to retirement, but there is no pot of money sitting there for me to draw on early. I think I could keep earning on repairs for those three extra years, yet I’d need a wage after the robots arrive unless something changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I’d ask Jo to teach me fault checks on the ground and ask the company whether paid inspection training has a place. I’d keep taking line shifts and put our cancelled television money toward the fuel debt. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for inspection posts while the field work still runs, and if I got one I’d learn its required screen with a person beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe a little more with five years to ask questions. But I still see the wage ending in 2034, and we have almost no reserve. It leaves me anxious rather than settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know what a loose connection sounds like, even if I’m not the fastest climber. A ground inspection role would use that, if one exists here. I don’t know how many openings there will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply retire at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I have not counted on it. The rent will keep coming and my partner’s shop pay is modest. I would want the numbers written out before saying we can stop my wage.

say: I’d demand an **honest crew plan** during the five-year warning.
I’d reject easy promises that everyone becomes a **supervisor**.
think: Three field years after 2031 might preserve my **line wage** temporarily.
I cannot assume **retirement** covers rent when robots arrive.
do: Learn **ground fault checks** from Jo while keeping line shifts.
Apply for **inspection posts** after 2031 if local vacancies appear.
Use cancelled television money against the **fuel debt**.
feel: Some breathing room, but **anxious** about 2034 income.
S3.quote: I would not promise that every worker can simply become a supervisor.
fieldNote: The later robot date gives Dana **working years**, although she does not treat them as a retirement guarantee.
Her interest in **ground inspection** grows from familiar fault checks, not enthusiasm for new screens.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and learn ground fault checks from Jo
Apply for local inspection posts after 2031
Apply cancelled television money to the fuel debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the depot that ten years gives us time to plan without making promises we cannot keep. I would want older junior hands included when training is offered. No one should assume we all leave at the same birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be 68 when the thinking AI comes and 71 when line robots arrive. I hope I can finish paid line work before a robot becomes a direct rival, but I have not checked whether we can live on retirement income. The risk is the ordinary bills between now and then, especially if hours weaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d sit with my partner and write down our actual retirement income and the rent, not a guess. I’d keep working line shifts and ask Jo for more practice on ground checks. In the first year after 2036, if I’m still on the payroll I’d take the field shifts available and decide with my partner whether our numbers allow me to leave before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to face this one. A decade could let me get to the end of working life, if the company keeps giving me hours and the sums work. The thin savings still leave me uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the numbers do not work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep applying for paid local work, including ground maintenance, while I can do it. I would not call it retirement just because I reach an age. Our grown children have their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to tell you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many line shifts it expects to keep through those ten years. If they only tell the older workers to wait, we cannot plan the rent. I want the numbers, even if they are rough.

say: I’d ask that **older junior hands** get training offers.
I’d say **retirement age** alone proves nothing about household income.
think: 2039 robots might arrive after my **line career**, if hours last.
Our **retirement sums** still need checking against rent.
do: Write down **retirement income and rent** with my partner now.
Keep taking **line shifts** and practise ground checks with Jo.
Apply for **paid local maintenance** if retirement numbers fall short.
feel: More capable of planning, though **uneasy** about current bills.
S4.quote: I would not call it retirement just because I reach an age.
fieldNote: Dana treats the decade as a possible **earnings bridge**, conditional on continuing shifts and affordable retirement.
She resists an automatic **retirement assumption** and wants actual income and rent written down.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and practise ground checks with Jo
Apply for paid local maintenance if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. We’ve saved less than one month of bills, and if the company stops needing hands by 2031, I cannot bridge that to retirement on my partner’s shop wages. A written promise of paid work through the change, or paid training for a real local role, would let me sleep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the older junior workers actually get the training places. People hear “apprenticeship” and picture a nineteen-year-old, not me turning up with sore knees and a certificate. I still want to earn my own pay.

headlineQuote: I still want to earn my own pay.
portrait: Dana is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered the trade late and learns new equipment slowly.
Her household has **under one month** of savings, and her partner’s shop wages cannot cover their bills alone.
She trusts **paid work and apprenticeships**, yet fears older beginners will be passed over for training.
Her worry peaks when **2031 robots** could remove the hands-on work that keeps her employed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Dana only three years before capable robots reach line work.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid-work promise** or funded training for an actual local job would make the transition bearable.
